title: Matinecock Tribal Nation
summary: The Matinecock Nation, an Algonquian people, has been the steward of northwestern Long Island since time immemorial. Their name, meaning “at the hilly land,” reflects an ancestral relationship with a territory extending along the North Shore from Flushing Bay to the Nissequogue River in present-day Smithtown. Long before European contact, Matinecock ancestors lived in extensive villages at Flushing, Port Washington, Glen Cove, Oyster Bay, Cold Spring Harbor, Huntington, and Northport, where numerous village sites.

why_this_matters: The Algonquian name Matinecock, meaning "at the hilly land," identifies the original stewards of a vast, resource-rich territory stretching from modern-day Flushing Bay all the way to the Nissequogue River. Remembering the true scale of this ancestral homeland challenges the historical erasure of Native peoples, ensuring that the deep Indigenous foundation of northwestern Long Island is not forgotten beneath today's urban sprawl.
introduction_content:
Although the names of Matinecock Sachems (leaders) appear on many colonial deeds, these documents were not understood by the Matinecock as final sales of the land—which cannot be owned—but rather as agreements to share resource rights (usufruct) in exchange for trade and protection. Among the first Native nations to experience calculated dispossession, disease, and the colonial “deed game,” the Matinecock nevertheless remained present. The so-called “myth of extinction” was a colonial construct used to undermine Indigenous land claims and erase evidence of continuous Matinecock presence.

Today, the Matinecock remain an identifiable and enduring people, maintaining their identity through kinship networks and tribal reunions in communities such as Flushing, Manhasset, Amityville, and Smithtown. Reconstituted in the 1950s through the Matinecock Longhouse by leaders including Sun Tama (Ann Harding Murdock) and Brown Thrush (Lila Elizabeth Harding), the Nation continues its cultural revitalization under the guidance of a Council of Elders, including Sachem Little Fox and Chief Osceola Townsend. Through ongoing efforts to protect sacred sites and reclaim cultural heritage, the Matinecock affirm their continued presence and sovereignty: they are still here.

You can attend the annual Native American Market and Social, organized by Matinecock artist Tecumseh Ceaser, held every December in Flushing, Queens, featuring Native artwork, drumming, singing, storytelling, and community gathering. The event brings together Indigenous artists, performers, and community members in celebration of Matinecock land, culture, and continued presence.
